subChunks.title: Images, Layers, Dockerfile & Orchestration Overview
subChunks.hookHtml: Containers solved the 'works on my machine' problem definitively. Every senior Java engineer needs to understand how Docker images are built, why layer caching matters, and how container orchestration enables the scaling and resilience patterns you've learned about in previous topics.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
What is a Container?

A container is a process running in an isolated namespace — its own filesystem, network, and process tree — sharing the host OS kernel. Lighter than a VM (no guest OS); starts in milliseconds; consistent across environments (dev, staging, prod).

A Docker image is a read-only template for creating containers. It consists of layers — each instruction in the Dockerfile adds a layer. Layers are cached: if a layer hasn't changed, Docker reuses the cached version in subsequent builds.

Dockerfile for a Spring Boot Application

# Layer 1: Base image (JDK 21, small Alpine-based)
FROM eclipse-temurin:21-jre-alpine

# Layer 2: Create non-root user (security best practice)
RUN addgroup -S appgroup && adduser -S appuser -G appgroup
USER appuser

# Layer 3: Set working directory
WORKDIR /app

# Layer 4: Copy the JAR (changes on every build — put last for cache efficiency)
COPY target/spell-service-1.0.jar app.jar

# Layer 5: Expose port (documentation only — does not publish)
EXPOSE 8080

# Run the application
ENTRYPOINT ["java", "-jar", "app.jar"]

Layer Caching — Ordering Matters

Layers are cached from top to bottom. Once a layer changes, all subsequent layers are invalidated. Put frequently-changing layers (your application JAR) last, and stable layers (base OS, dependencies) first.

For Java services, use a multi-stage build or Spring Boot's layered JAR to separate dependencies from application code — dependency layer changes only when pom.xml changes, not on every code change.

# Layered JAR build — dependencies cached separately
FROM eclipse-temurin:21-jdk-alpine AS builder
COPY . .
RUN mvn package -DskipTests && java -Djarmode=layertools -jar target/*.jar extract

FROM eclipse-temurin:21-jre-alpine
COPY --from=builder dependencies/ ./
COPY --from=builder snapshot-dependencies/ ./
COPY --from=builder application/ ./
ENTRYPOINT ["java", "org.springframework.boot.loader.JarLauncher"]

Container Security Basics

  • Never run as root — use a non-root user in Dockerfile
  • Use minimal base images (Alpine, Distroless) to reduce attack surface
  • Scan images for vulnerabilities (Docker Scout, Trivy, Snyk)
  • Don't put secrets in the image — use environment variables or secrets management

Orchestration Overview

Container orchestration manages the lifecycle of many containers across multiple hosts: scheduling, scaling, health checks, rolling deployments, service discovery, and load balancing.

Kubernetes (K8s): the industry standard. Key concepts: Pod (one or more containers), Deployment (desired state for a set of Pods), Service (stable network endpoint), Ingress (HTTP routing), ConfigMap/Secret (configuration injection).

Cloud Run / App Engine / ECS: managed container services where you give the platform an image and it handles orchestration. Lower operational overhead; less control. Appropriate for teams that don't want to operate Kubernetes.

storyBeats.text: Before containers, deploying the Academy's spell service required: install Java, configure application server, set environment variables, copy config files, start the process. On each of 20 servers. Differently, because each server had a slightly different history. Containers replaced all of that with one Docker image and one command: docker run.

storyBeats.speaker: Infrastructure Architect Sola
storyBeats.text: A Docker image is a reproducible build artifact. The same image that passes tests in CI is exactly the image that runs in production — not a copy, not a rebuild. Same filesystem, same dependencies, same JVM version. The environment stops being a variable. That elimination of environmental drift is what containers actually solve.

storyBeats.speaker: Infrastructure Architect Sola
storyBeats.text: Layer caching is one of the most practical things to understand about Docker. Every time you put COPY target/app.jar at line 5 and your dependency installation at line 12, you throw away the dependency cache on every build. Reverse it. Put the things that change least at the top. Put the application JAR at the bottom. Builds go from 4 minutes to 20 seconds.

storyBeats.speaker: Why ordering matters for cache
storyBeats.text:
# BAD — JAR copied before dependencies installed
FROM eclipse-temurin:21-jre-alpine
COPY target/app.jar app.jar         # changes every build — invalidates everything below
RUN apk add --no-cache curl          # re-runs on EVERY build, even if unchanged

# GOOD — stable layers first
FROM eclipse-temurin:21-jre-alpine
RUN apk add --no-cache curl          # cached — only runs when base image changes
COPY target/app.jar app.jar          # last — invalidates nothing below it

storyBeats.speaker: Infrastructure Architect Sola
storyBeats.text: For a senior engineer in 2025, the practical decision is usually not 'Kubernetes vs not Kubernetes.' It's 'do we need the control and flexibility of Kubernetes, or does Cloud Run or ECS serve us with less operational overhead?' If your team has fewer than three people managing infrastructure, managed container platforms are often the right answer.

learningObjectives: Explain the difference between a Docker image and a container, and what layers are
Write a correct Dockerfile for a Spring Boot application following security and cache best practices
Explain why Dockerfile instruction order affects build speed via layer caching
Describe the key Kubernetes concepts (Pod, Deployment, Service) at an overview level
commonMistakes: Copying the application JAR before installing dependencies — forces dependency installation to re-run on every code change
Running containers as root — security vulnerability; use a non-root user
Storing secrets in the image (ENV PASSWORD=...) — visible in image history; use runtime injection
Using large base images (ubuntu, openjdk:latest) when alpine or distroless would suffice — inflates image size and attack surface
assessmentCriteria: Can write a Dockerfile for a Spring Boot JAR with correct layer order, non-root user, and minimal base image
Can explain why layer caching is invalidated and how to order instructions to maximise cache hits
Can explain what a Kubernetes Deployment and Service are and what problem each solves
Can identify at least two security issues in a given Dockerfile and propose fixes
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain Docker to a developer who has only deployed applications by SSHing into a server. What is an image? What is a layer? Why does the order of Dockerfile instructions matter? Why should they care?
subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
Answer the following Dockerfile and container questions:

  1. Below is a Dockerfile with three problems. Identify each one and write the corrected version: 
    FROM openjdk:17
USER root
COPY target/app.jar .
RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y curl
ENTRYPOINT ["java", "-jar", "app.jar"]
  2. Your build currently takes 4 minutes. The only change between builds is your application source code. The Dockerfile has: base image → copy pom.xml → copy src → run mvn package. Re-order and explain why it speeds up the build.
  3. Your Spring Boot app needs a database password at runtime. List two ways to provide it that do NOT involve storing it in the Docker image.
subChunks.guidedPracticeModelAnswer:
1. Three problems in the original Dockerfile:
   a) `openjdk:17` — large, unsupported image. Fix: use eclipse-temurin:21-jre-alpine (smaller, current, JRE-only).
   b) `USER root` — running as root is a security risk. Fix: create and use a non-root user.
   c) `COPY target/app.jar` before `apt-get install` — JAR changes invalidate the curl installation cache on every build. Fix: put RUN (stable) before COPY (frequently-changing).
   
   Corrected Dockerfile:
   FROM eclipse-temurin:21-jre-alpine
   RUN addgroup -S app && adduser -S app -G app
   RUN apk add --no-cache curl
   USER app
   WORKDIR /app
   COPY target/app.jar app.jar
   ENTRYPOINT ["java", "-jar", "app.jar"]

2. Reordered for cache efficiency:
   FROM eclipse-temurin:21-jre-alpine
   WORKDIR /app
   COPY pom.xml .           # changes rarely — cached
   RUN mvn dependency:go-offline  # download deps once — cached when pom unchanged
   COPY src ./src           # changes often
   RUN mvn package -DskipTests    # only re-runs when src changes
   COPY target/*.jar app.jar
   ENTRYPOINT ["java","-jar","app.jar"]
   
   Why faster: dependency download (slowest step) is cached. Only the mvn compile and package re-run on code changes — typically seconds instead of minutes.

3. Two ways to provide the DB password without embedding it:
   a) Environment variable at runtime: docker run -e DB_PASSWORD=secret myapp
      The app reads System.getenv("DB_PASSWORD"). Secret never in image; injected at runtime.
   b) Secrets management: Kubernetes Secret or AWS Secrets Manager / GCP Secret Manager.
      Container retrieves the secret at startup from the secrets service using IAM credentials (not hardcoded).
      Rotation and auditing are handled centrally.
subChunks.soloPracticeHtml:
Design the containerisation strategy for the Academy's full stack: spell-service (Spring Boot JAR, port 8080), postgres database, and redis cache. Answer:

  1. Write a docker-compose.yml sketch (service names, images, ports, environment, depends_on) for local development
  2. For the spell-service Dockerfile, describe the multi-stage build that separates the Maven build from the runtime image
  3. For production on Kubernetes, name the resources you would create for the spell-service (at minimum) and what each one does
  4. What is the biggest difference between docker-compose (local dev) and Kubernetes (production) in terms of responsibility?
subChunks.modelAnswer:
1. docker-compose.yml sketch:
services:
  spell-service:
    build: .
    ports: ["8080:8080"]
    environment:
      SPRING_DATASOURCE_URL: jdbc:postgresql://postgres:5432/academy
      SPRING_DATASOURCE_PASSWORD: ${DB_PASSWORD}
      SPRING_REDIS_HOST: redis
    depends_on: [postgres, redis]
  
  postgres:
    image: postgres:16-alpine
    environment: {POSTGRES_DB: academy, POSTGRES_PASSWORD: ${DB_PASSWORD}}
    volumes: ["pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data"]
  
  redis:
    image: redis:7-alpine
    ports: ["6379:6379"]

volumes: {pgdata: {}}

2. Multi-stage build:
FROM eclipse-temurin:21-jdk-alpine AS builder
WORKDIR /app
COPY pom.xml .
RUN mvn dependency:go-offline
COPY src ./src
RUN mvn package -DskipTests

FROM eclipse-temurin:21-jre-alpine
RUN addgroup -S app && adduser -S app -G app && chown -R app:app /app
USER app
WORKDIR /app
COPY --from=builder /app/target/*.jar app.jar
ENTRYPOINT ["java","-jar","app.jar"]
# JDK only in builder stage — runtime image contains only JRE, no Maven, no source

3. Kubernetes resources for spell-service:
- Deployment: defines the desired Pod spec (image, replicas=3, resource limits, env vars from Secrets)
- Service (ClusterIP): stable internal DNS endpoint (spell-service:8080) for other services to call
- Ingress: external HTTP routing — routes /api/spells to spell-service:8080
- HorizontalPodAutoscaler: scales replicas 2–10 based on CPU utilisation
- Secret: holds DB password, JWT secret — injected as env vars into the Deployment
- ConfigMap: non-secret config (log level, feature flags)

4. Key difference:
docker-compose: you manage the networking, volumes, and startup order manually. Everything runs on one machine. No automatic recovery if a container crashes (unless restart: always set). Suitable for local dev and simple staging.
Kubernetes: the platform manages scheduling across multiple nodes, automatic restart on crash, rolling updates, self-healing, horizontal scaling, and service discovery. More complex to operate; far more capable. Production needs this operational responsibility handled by the platform.

questions.correctAnswer: A read-only filesystem change produced by a single Dockerfile instruction, cached and reused across builds
questions.explanationHtml: Each instruction in a Dockerfile (RUN, COPY, ADD) creates a new read-only layer on top of the previous one. When a layer hasn't changed, Docker reuses the cached version — skipping the rebuild of that layer and all layers before it. Images are stacks of these layers; containers add a thin writable layer on top when they run.

questions.questionHtml: A Dockerfile has these instructions in order: COPY pom.xml → RUN mvn dependency:resolve → COPY src → RUN mvn package. Why is this ordering better than: COPY src → RUN mvn package?
options: The dependency download layer is cached and only re-runs when pom.xml changes, not on every code change
Maven runs faster when dependencies are resolved in a separate step
The JVM starts faster with pre-resolved dependencies
questions.correctAnswer: The dependency download layer is cached and only re-runs when pom.xml changes, not on every code change
questions.explanationHtml: By copying pom.xml and resolving dependencies as a separate layer before copying src, the expensive dependency download is only re-run when pom.xml changes. When only application source code changes, Docker uses the cached dependency layer and only re-runs the compile/package step. This turns a 4-minute build into a 30-second build for typical code changes.

questions.questionHtml: In Kubernetes, what is the difference between a Pod and a Deployment?
options: A Pod is the network layer; a Deployment is the application layer
A Pod is the smallest deployable unit (one or more containers); a Deployment manages a set of identical Pods with desired replica count, rolling update strategy, and self-healing
A Deployment runs on one machine; a Pod runs across multiple machines
They are synonyms for the same concept
questions.correctAnswer: A Pod is the smallest deployable unit (one or more containers); a Deployment manages a set of identical Pods with desired replica count, rolling update strategy, and self-healing
questions.explanationHtml: A Pod is the atomic unit of Kubernetes — one or more containers that share a network and filesystem. A Deployment is a higher-level resource that declares: 'I want 3 replicas of this Pod, and if one dies, create a new one.' Deployments manage Pod lifecycle, rolling updates, and rollbacks. You almost never create Pods directly — you create Deployments that manage Pods for you.
